question: Two parabolas have equations \(y = x^2 + ax + b\) and \(y = x^2 + cx + d,\) where \(a,\) \(b,\) \(c,\) and \(d\) are integers (not necessarily different), each chosen independently by rolling a fair six-sided die. What is the probability that the parabolas have at least one point in common?
solution:
At a common point, the two expressions for \(y\) are equal. Their identical quadratic terms cancel:
\[
x^2+ax+b=x^2+cx+d
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(a-c)x=d-b.
\]
If \(a\ne c\), this equation has the real solution \(x=(d-b)/(a-c)\), so the parabolas intersect. If \(a=c\), they coincide when \(b=d\) and have no common point when \(b\ne d\). Thus failure occurs exactly when \(a=c\) and \(b\ne d\).

Of the \(36\) equally likely ordered results for \((a,c)\), exactly \(6\) have equal entries, so \(P(a=c)=1/6\). Similarly, \(P(b\ne d)=30/36=5/6\). These conditions involve separate independent pairs of die rolls, so
\[
P(\text{no common point})=\frac16\cdot\frac56=\frac5{36}.
\]
Taking the complementary probability gives
\[
P(\text{at least one common point})
=1-\frac5{36}=\boxed{\frac{31}{36}},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
